Using the PSL framework described above, uncertainty estimates are fairly straightforward due to the limited dimensionality of the solution space, where a single source position and activity atop a constant background are fit and the Fisher information estimate can be readily applied to achieve statistical error estimates. Those are further modified (1) to account for effects from voxel discretization and (2) to account for systematic errors arising from the difference between the true source positions being different from the centers of voxels, which impact activity estimates through the 1/r2 term. Conversely, there has been no effort to quantify and incorporate errors associated with background variations. To do so would require further advances in full-spectrum analyses, discussed below. Approaches for estimating errors associated with mapping distributed sources have also been examined,albeitnon-exhaustively. Bayesianframeworkscanallowfortheextractionoferrorbound estimates through the ‘credible interval’ of the posterior solution, e.g., as was developed by Pereyra et al. [41]. However, in our experience applying this approach to both real and simulated data, the limits are quite broad, which we have attributed to the lack of machinery to incorporate the correlatednatureofreconstructedpixels/voxelsintheimagespace. To‘build-in’somecorrelations, wehaveoftenresortedtore-runningthePereyraalgorithmwithmuchlargervoxels(‘super-voxels’), through summing subsets of columns of the system matrix prior to producing credible intervals. This process results in less conservative error estimates, but also still omits spatial detail in the error estimates of the solution space and continues to ignore correlations between super-voxels.
